items.explanation: The passage says meritocracy promises reward for talent and effort, yet talent is shaped by schooling, health and networks, so the ladder is not equally long for everyone and success is often credited to merit when luck played a large part. It does not claim effort is irrelevant or that meritocracy has no appeal.
options: Meritocracy is a perfect system in which everyone starts from exactly the same place
Meritocracy fails because talent and effort play no part in success at all
Meritocracy is unfair only because some people are naturally lazy
Meritocracy promises reward for talent and effort, yet talent is shaped by unequal schooling, health and networks, so success is often credited to merit when luck played a large part
Meritocracy has no appeal to anyone, because no one believes in fairness
items.passage: Meritocracy is an attractive idea. It promises that success will go to those who deserve it, to the talented and the hardworking, rather than to those born into privilege. The promise is so appealing that questioning it can feel like an attack on fairness itself. Yet the idea contains a quiet contradiction. Talent is not distributed by lottery alone; it is shaped by schooling, by health, by nutrition, by the books in a house and the networks around it. Effort, too, is easier when life is stable and harder when it is not. Two children of equal ability, born into different circumstances, will not have equal chances to show that ability, and the one who succeeds may sincerely believe the success was earned entirely by merit. The problem is not that talent and effort do not matter. They do, and a society that ignored them would be unjust in a different way. The problem is that meritocracy, by praising the winners, also blames the losers. If success is proof of merit, then failure must be proof of its absence, and the poor can be told that their poverty is their own fault. A fairer society would not abandon the idea of rewarding merit, but it would be honest about how much of success is luck, and it would refuse to use merit as a reason to abandon those who, through no fault of their own, started further back. The ladder may be real, but it is not the same length for everyone, and pretending otherwise makes the climb harder for those already at a disadvantage. Examinations are the clearest example, because they are designed to measure merit, yet they measure, in large part, the resources that went into preparation. A student who attends a good school, has a quiet room to study in, and can afford a tutor will perform better than a student of equal ability who lacks those things, and the examination will record the difference as a difference in merit. The system then rewards the first student with a place at a good university, which provides further resources, and the gap widens. None of this means examinations should be abolished, but it means their results should be read with humility, as a measure of performance under unequal conditions, not as a verdict on a person's worth, and a society that forgets that distinction will mistake privilege for talent.
items.question: What is the author's central criticism of meritocracy?

items.explanation: The passage says if success is proof of merit then failure must be proof of its absence, so the poor can be told their poverty is their own fault. That is the blame mechanism the author identifies, not a claim that winners are lazy or that effort does not matter.
options: Meritocracy makes winners lazy, because they believe they have already proved themselves
Meritocracy, by praising winners, also blames losers, since failure is read as proof that merit was absent
Meritocracy makes losers more successful, because blame motivates them to work harder
Meritocracy has no effect on how people explain poverty
Meritocracy proves that poverty is always caused by laziness
items.question: How does meritocracy, according to the author, affect those who fail?

items.explanation: The author says a fairer society would keep rewarding merit but be honest about luck and refuse to use merit as a reason to abandon those who started further back. Abandoning merit, ignoring luck, and blaming the poor all contradict that proposal.
options: Keep rewarding merit, but be honest about how much of success is luck, and refuse to use merit as a reason to abandon those who started further back
Abandon the idea of rewarding merit entirely and reward everyone equally regardless of effort
Pretend that the ladder is the same length for everyone, so that no one feels disadvantaged
Use merit as a reason to abandon those who started further back, since they have proved they lack merit
Ignore luck entirely and judge every outcome as pure merit
items.question: What does the author propose as a fairer approach than pure meritocracy?

items.explanation: The passage says language does not merely describe the world, it decides what can be said, and those who control terms control the argument, with examples of tax relief, collateral damage and downsizing. It does not claim language is neutral, that words have fixed meanings, or that euphemism is harmless.
options: Language is a neutral tool that merely describes the world as it is
Words have fixed meanings that never change with context
Euphemism is harmless, because everyone understands what it really means
Language is only important in poetry and has no effect on politics
Language does not merely describe the world; it decides what can be said, and those who control the terms control the argument
items.passage: Language is often treated as a neutral tool, a way of describing a world that exists independently of words. Yet the words we choose decide what can be said, and therefore what can be thought. To call a tax cut relief is to imply that tax is an affliction, and that cutting it is a cure. To call civilian deaths collateral damage is to make them sound like an unavoidable side effect, rather than a moral catastrophe. To call a firing a downsizing is to hide the human cost behind a technical term. None of this is accidental. Those who control the terms of a debate often control its outcome, because the terms decide which questions are legitimate and which are ruled out before they are asked. Power, in this account, is not only exercised through laws and armies. It is exercised through vocabulary, through the slow work of making some descriptions seem natural and others seem extreme. The remedy is not to find a perfectly neutral language, since no such language exists, but to notice the work that words are doing. When a phrase feels inevitable, ask who benefits from its inevitability. When a euphemism smooths over a harm, ask what the plain description would sound like. Language will always shape thought, but thought can also, with effort, reshape language, and that effort is one of the few defences a society has against being governed by words it did not choose. News headlines show the same mechanism at work every day, because a headline must compress a complex event into a few words, and the words chosen decide how the event is understood. A protest can be described as a riot or as a demonstration, a tax as a burden or as a contribution, a migrant as a stranger or as a neighbour, and each choice frames the story before the reader has read a single sentence. Readers who are aware of this can seek out other framings, compare them, and form a judgement that is their own. Readers who are not aware may believe they are forming an opinion, when in fact they are repeating the framing they were given, and that is why media literacy, the ability to notice the work words are doing, is now as important as the ability to read them.
items.question: What is the author's central claim about language and power?

items.explanation: The passage gives tax relief implying tax is an affliction, collateral damage making civilian deaths sound like a side effect, and downsizing hiding the human cost of firing. Those examples show terms deciding which questions are legitimate, not that euphemisms are harmless or language is neutral.
options: Tax relief, collateral damage and downsizing are neutral technical terms with no effect on thought
Tax relief, collateral damage and downsizing are examples of how chosen terms frame a subject, imply a judgement, and hide human cost
Tax relief, collateral damage and downsizing prove that language is perfectly neutral
Tax relief, collateral damage and downsizing are used only in poetry, not in politics
Tax relief, collateral damage and downsizing show that euphemism is always harmless
items.question: Why does the author cite tax relief, collateral damage and downsizing?

items.explanation: The author says there is no perfectly neutral language, so the remedy is to notice the work words do, ask who benefits when a phrase feels inevitable, and ask what the plain description would sound like. Banning euphemisms, finding a neutral language, and accepting inevitability all contradict that advice.
options: Find a perfectly neutral language that describes the world without any framing
Ban all euphemisms by law, so that no one can ever use them
Notice the work words are doing, ask who benefits when a phrase feels inevitable, and ask what the plain description would sound like
Accept that language is inevitable and never question the terms of a debate
Refuse to use language at all in political discussion
items.question: What remedy does the author propose for the power of language?

items.explanation: The passage says those who emitted least suffer most, while those who emitted most are best protected, so the question is who pays for a crisis they did not cause and who decides. It is not a purely technical or future-only problem, and richer countries are not the main sufferers.
options: Climate change affects everyone equally, regardless of where they live or how much they emitted
Climate change is a purely technical problem with no moral dimension
Climate change will only affect future generations, not people alive today
Those who emitted least suffer most, while those who emitted most are best protected, so climate policy is a question of who pays for a crisis they did not cause
Richer countries suffer most from climate change, because they have the most to lose
items.passage: Climate change is often discussed as a technical problem, a matter of parts per million and degrees of warming. Yet its deepest questions are moral. Those who have emitted least, farmers in low lying deltas, herders in drying grasslands, islanders whose homes may disappear, are often those who will suffer most. Those who have emitted most, wealthy societies with air conditioning, insurance and the means to move, are often best protected from the consequences of their own emissions. This asymmetry is what makes climate policy so difficult. It is not only a question of how much to cut, but of who should cut, who should pay, and who should decide. A policy that asks the poorest to bear the cost of a crisis they did not cause is not merely inefficient; it is unjust. A policy that asks the richest to pay for the damage they caused is not merely fair; it is also the only kind that the poorest will accept as legitimate. The difficulty is that the rich, who must pay, are also those with the most power to resist paying, while the poor, who must be protected, have the least power to demand protection. Justice, in this context, is not an extra demand added to climate policy. It is the condition without which climate policy cannot work, because a policy perceived as unjust will be resisted, evaded and ultimately abandoned, while a policy perceived as fair has a chance of being sustained across the decades that climate action requires. Adaptation funding raises the same question in practical form, because the money for sea walls, for drought resistant crops and for relocating villages must come from somewhere, and the countries that need it most are often those least able to pay for it. A fund that is financed by voluntary contributions from wealthy countries may be generous in good years and empty in bad ones, while a fund financed by a levy on emissions would be more stable, but harder to agree. The choice between those designs is not technical but moral, because it decides who bears the cost of a crisis, and whether the burden falls on those who caused it or on those who suffer from it. A climate policy that ignores that choice may succeed on paper, by cutting emissions, while failing in practice, by losing the consent of those it was meant to protect.
items.question: What is the author's central claim about climate justice?

items.explanation: The passage says the rich who must pay have the most power to resist, while the poor who must be protected have the least power to demand protection. That power asymmetry is the difficulty identified, not a lack of technology, money, or scientific agreement.
options: The rich, who must pay, have the most power to resist paying, while the poor, who must be protected, have the least power to demand protection
There is no technology available to cut emissions at all
There is no money available anywhere to pay for climate action
Scientists disagree completely about whether climate change is happening
The poor have more political power than the rich in climate negotiations
items.question: What difficulty does the author identify in achieving climate justice?

items.explanation: The author says justice is the condition without which climate policy cannot work, because a policy perceived as unjust will be resisted, evaded and abandoned, while a fair one has a chance of being sustained. Justice is therefore not an extra demand but a precondition for success.
options: Justice is an extra demand that makes climate policy harder and should be set aside
Justice is irrelevant to whether climate policy succeeds or fails
Justice is a luxury that only wealthy societies can afford to consider
Justice is a purely moral idea with no practical effect on policy
Justice is the condition without which climate policy cannot work, because an unjust policy will be resisted and abandoned while a fair one may be sustained
items.question: Why does the author say justice is not an extra demand added to climate policy?

items.explanation: The passage says surveillance changes behaviour even when no one is punished, because people who know they may be watched behave as if they are always watched, internalising the watcher and censoring themselves. It is not only about catching criminals, and the effect is not limited to the guilty.
options: Surveillance affects only people who have committed a crime
Surveillance has no effect on behaviour unless a person is actually punished
Surveillance changes behaviour even when no one is punished, because people who know they may be watched behave as if they are always watched and censor themselves
Surveillance makes people more honest, because they know they are being watched
Surveillance affects only the behaviour of criminals, not of ordinary citizens
items.passage: Surveillance is often defended on the grounds that it catches criminals, and that the innocent have nothing to hide. That defence misses the deeper effect of being watched. A person who knows she may be watched behaves differently from a person who knows she is alone, even when she has done nothing wrong. She chooses her words more carefully, avoids unpopular opinions, and thinks twice before reading something unusual. The watcher need not punish anyone for this effect to occur; the possibility of being watched is enough. Over time, the effect becomes internal. People stop needing an external watcher, because they have internalised one, censoring themselves before any authority intervenes. A society in which everyone behaves as if watched is not necessarily a safer society. It may be a quieter one, but quiet is not the same as safety, and a society that has lost the habit of dissent, of experiment, of saying the unpopular thing, has lost something that safety alone cannot replace. Privacy, in this account, is not a luxury for those with secrets to hide. It is the condition that allows people to think, to doubt and to dissent without fear, and without it, freedom becomes a performance, something people do when they believe they are being observed, rather than something they possess when they are alone. Workplace monitoring extends the same logic into offices and factories, where keystrokes, locations and even eye movements can be tracked in the name of productivity. An employee who knows she is monitored may work faster, but she may also avoid taking risks, avoid asking questions, and avoid the informal conversations in which new ideas are born. The organisation gains a measure of activity and loses a measure of creativity, and it may not notice the loss, because creativity is harder to count than keystrokes. A wiser employer would monitor outcomes rather than movements, trusting employees to find their own way to a result, and would accept that some unmonitored time is not wasted time but the space in which thinking happens, and in which a worker can be alone with a problem long enough to solve it.
items.question: What is the author's central claim about surveillance?

items.explanation: The passage says privacy allows people to think, doubt and dissent without fear, and without it freedom becomes a performance done when observed rather than possessed when alone. It is not a luxury for criminals, and it is not irrelevant to freedom.
options: Privacy is a luxury for people with secrets to hide, and has no value for the innocent
Privacy is the condition that allows people to think, doubt and dissent without fear, and without it freedom becomes a performance rather than something possessed when alone
Privacy is irrelevant to freedom, because freedom is only about laws, not about being watched
Privacy makes society less safe, because it allows criminals to hide
Privacy is only important for people who hold unpopular opinions
items.question: How does the author define the value of privacy?

items.explanation: The author says a watched society may be quieter but quiet is not the same as safety, and a society that has lost dissent, experiment and unpopular speech has lost something safety cannot replace. Surveillance is not said to guarantee safety, and quiet is not equated with safety.
options: A quiet society is always a safe society, because silence proves that crime has been prevented
Surveillance guarantees safety, because watched people never commit crimes
A society that has lost dissent has lost nothing of value, as long as it is safe
A watched society may be quieter, but quiet is not the same as safety, and losing the habit of dissent is a loss safety alone cannot replace
Dissent is dangerous and should be discouraged in the interests of safety
items.question: What does the author mean by saying quiet is not the same as safety?

items.explanation: The passage says a perfect copy can be indistinguishable yet the original matters because of its history, the hand that made it, and the time it has survived, so authenticity is about provenance and human touch rather than visual difference alone. It does not claim copies are worthless or that originals are always better visually.
options: A perfect copy can be indistinguishable from an original, yet the original matters because of its history, the hand that made it, and the time it has survived
A perfect copy is always more valuable than an original, because it is newer
Authenticity is purely a matter of visual appearance, so a copy that looks identical is authentic
Originals have no value at all once a perfect copy exists
Authenticity is irrelevant to art, because only the image matters
items.passage: In an age of perfect reproduction, the question of authenticity has become urgent. A photograph can be copied a million times without loss, a painting can be reproduced so accurately that experts struggle to tell the copy from the original, and a piece of music can be heard in exactly the same form by listeners on opposite sides of the world. Why, then, does the original still matter? Part of the answer is history. The original was present at a moment that cannot be repeated; it bears the marks of the hand that made it, the accidents of its creation, the repairs of centuries. A copy, however perfect, has a different history, and that history matters to how we value it. Another part is scarcity. An original is one of a kind, while a copy can be multiplied without limit, and scarcity, for better or worse, shapes desire. But the deepest part is human. We value the original because it is a trace of another person, a proof that someone was there, that a hand moved in a particular way at a particular time. A copy can show us what the original looks like, but it cannot show us that it was made. Authenticity, in this account, is not a property of the image alone. It is a property of the relationship between the object, its maker and its history, and that relationship cannot be reproduced, however perfect the copy. Digital art raises the question in a new form, because a digital image can be copied perfectly and distributed instantly, yet artists now sell certificates of authenticity that claim a particular copy is the original. The certificate does not change the image, which remains identical to every other copy, but it changes the relationship between the owner, the artist and the work, creating scarcity where none existed before. Some see this as a clever solution to an old problem, a way for digital artists to earn a living. Others see it as a sign that authenticity has become a fiction, a story told about an object rather than a property of it. Either way, the debate shows that authenticity was never only about the object itself, but about the human relationships that surround it, and those relationships can be created, bought and sold, even when the image cannot be distinguished from its copies.
items.question: According to the passage, why does an original still matter when a perfect copy exists?

items.explanation: The passage says authenticity is a property of the relationship between the object, its maker and its history, which cannot be reproduced however perfect the copy. It is not a property of the image alone, nor is it about newness or scarcity alone.
options: Authenticity is a property of the image alone, so a perfect copy is authentic
Authenticity is about newness, so the newest copy is the most authentic
Authenticity is a property of the relationship between the object, its maker and its history, which cannot be reproduced however perfect the copy
Authenticity is about scarcity alone, so any scarce object is authentic regardless of its history
Authenticity can be reproduced perfectly, as long as the copy is accurate enough
items.question: How does the author define authenticity?

items.explanation: The passage says we value the original because it is a trace of another person, proof that someone was there and a hand moved in a particular way at a particular time. A copy shows what the original looks like but cannot show that it was made, so the human trace is the deepest reason.
options: Because originals are always more beautiful than copies
Because originals are always more expensive than copies
Because scarcity alone makes any object valuable, regardless of who made it
Because a copy can show what the original looks like, but it cannot show that a hand made it at a particular time
Because copies are always flawed in ways that experts can detect
items.question: What is the deepest reason the author gives for valuing an original?

items.explanation: The poem shows the weaver's hands remembering patterns her mind has forgotten, the shuttle moving on its own, and the cloth holding what words could not, so skill lives in the body and in the work, not only in conscious memory. It is not about forgetting entirely, anger, or a complaint about weaving.
options: The weaver has forgotten how to weave and is making mistakes
The weaver's hands remember patterns her mind has forgotten, showing that skill and memory live in the body and in the work itself
The weaver is angry at the loom for breaking down
The weaver is trying to sell the cloth for a high price
The weaver has never learned to weave and is pretending to do so
items.passage: Her hands remembered what her mind had forgotten, / the pattern of the border, the twist of the thread, / the way the shuttle moved when the light was low, / and the cloth grew, row by row, in the quiet room. // She did not count the threads, or name the colours, / and the shuttle flew like a bird that knows its way, / returning always to the hand that had thrown it. // The cloth she wove was not for sale, or for show, / it was for the daughter who had gone away, / for the winter that would come, for the hands / that would one day hold it and remember her. // When she died, the cloth remained, / folded, in a drawer, smelling of woodsmoke, / and her daughter, holding it, understood at last / that some things are not taught, but woven, / in the hands, in the quiet, in the work itself.
items.question: What does the weaver's hands remembering what her mind forgot chiefly suggest?

items.explanation: The cloth remaining after her death, folded and smelling of woodsmoke, and the daughter understanding that some things are woven in the hands, shows the work outliving its maker as a form of memory. It is not a sale, a complaint, or a sign the cloth was unfinished.
options: The cloth was unfinished and therefore worthless
The cloth was made only to be sold for money
The cloth was a mistake that the weaver regretted
The cloth outlives its maker as a form of memory, carrying what words and conscious teaching could not
The cloth was forgotten in a drawer and never found again
items.question: The image of the cloth remaining after the weaver's death most nearly suggests that

items.explanation: The argument assumes regular exercise itself causes the lower stress rather than other differences between exercisers and non-exercisers explaining both. The other options are stronger claims the argument does not need, such as every exerciser being stress free or exercise being the only cause.
options: Every person who exercises regularly is completely free of stress
Exercise is the only cause of low stress in any population
Regular exercise itself causes the lower stress, rather than other differences between exercisers and non-exercisers
People who do not exercise never experience low stress
Exercise is more important than sleep, diet and work conditions combined
items.question: A study finds people who exercise regularly report lower stress than people who do not. A writer concludes that exercise reduces stress. Which assumption is required?

items.explanation: If a competitor closed at the same time, the closure is an alternative cause for the rise in customers, weakening the claim that the new menu alone caused it. Customer liking, the menu being popular, and the chef's experience are weaker or irrelevant.
options: A nearby competitor restaurant closed at the same time as the new menu was introduced
Some customers said they liked the new menu
The new menu was popular with younger customers in particular
The chef had ten years of experience in cooking
The restaurant hired two new waiters during the same period
items.question: A restaurant introduces a new menu and finds customer numbers rise by 25 percent in two months. The owner argues the new menu caused the rise. Which finding most weakens the argument?

items.explanation: Because the tea drinkers also differ in income and access to healthcare, those differences could explain the health gap, so the study cannot establish that tea alone caused it. It does not prove tea has no effect, nor that non-drinkers will necessarily be less healthy.
options: Drinking herbal tea alone causes better health, regardless of income or healthcare
Herbal tea has no effect on health at all
People who do not drink herbal tea will necessarily be less healthy
Income and healthcare are irrelevant to health
The study cannot establish that herbal tea alone caused the difference, because the groups also differed in income and access to healthcare
items.question: A study finds people who drink herbal tea daily are healthier on average than those who do not. However, the tea drinkers also have higher incomes and better access to healthcare. Which conclusion is best supported?

items.explanation: Obdurate means stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or course of action, so stubborn is closest. Flexible and yielding are opposites, gentle concerns manner rather than stubbornness, and hasty means acting too quickly.
options: Flexible
Stubborn
Yielding
Gentle
Hasty
items.question: Choose the word closest in meaning to OBDURATE.

items.explanation: The number of students takes has, since number is singular, while the other options mismatch subjects and verbs. Each takes is, neither the students nor the teacher takes is, and the team along with the coach takes is, not are.
options: The number of students has increased this year.
The number of students have increased this year.
Each of the students are present today.
Neither the students nor the teacher are responsible.
The team, along with the coach, are travelling tomorrow.
items.question: Which sentence is grammatically correct?

items.explanation: The order must open with the old clock, then its stopping, then the watchmaker's decision, then the town listening, then the lesson, giving A, C, B, D, E. Starting with E states the lesson first, and D before B has the town listening before the clock is repaired.
options: A, B, C, D, E
C, A, B, D, E
A, C, B, D, E
E, A, C, B, D
B, A, C, E, D
items.question: Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph. (A) The old clock in the square had kept time for a hundred years. (B) He repaired it in silence, without asking for payment, and wound it by hand. (C) One winter morning it stopped, and the town fell silent with it. (D) Within a week, the town was listening to its own time again, and the square was full of voices. (E) Time, the watchmaker learned, is not kept by a clock but by the people who listen to it. Choose the correct order.

items.explanation: The sequence runs from the letter arriving, to the boy reading it, to the train leaving, to the mother waiting, to the lesson that a letter can be a journey, giving C, A, B, D, E. Opening with E states the lesson first, and B before A puts the train before the letter is read.
options: C, B, A, D, E
A, C, B, D, E
B, C, A, D, E
C, A, B, D, E
E, C, A, B, D
items.question: Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph. (A) The boy read it three times, once for the news, once for the handwriting, and once for the silence between the lines. (B) The train left at dawn, carrying him to a city he had never seen. (C) The letter arrived on a Tuesday, in an envelope with no stamp. (D) His mother stood at the gate until the train was out of sight, and then went back inside. (E) A letter, the boy learned, can be a journey in itself. Choose the correct order.

items.explanation: The sentence needs a word for excessive praise and a word for harsh blame: fulsome for the praise and censorious for the blame fits, while laudatory is praise not blame, and vituperative is blame not praise. The other pairs place praise and blame in the wrong order or mix two praises.
options: censorious and fulsome
fulsome and censorious
laudatory and censorious
fulsome and laudatory
censorious and vituperative
items.question: Fill in the blanks with the most appropriate pair. The speech was ______ in its praise of the leader, yet ______ in its blame of his critics, leaving listeners unsure whether it was a tribute or an attack. (1) fulsome (2) censorious (3) laudatory (4) vituperative

items.explanation: A small boat labelled Courage sailing toward a huge wave labelled Fear, with the sailor smiling rather than turning back, shows that courage is not the absence of fear but action in spite of it. The literal readings miss the labels, and turning back or waiting for calm are the opposite of the point.
options: Fear should always be avoided by turning back immediately
Courage means never feeling fear at all
The sailor should wait for the wave to disappear before sailing
Small boats should never sail toward large waves
Courage is not the absence of fear, but action in spite of fear, even when the fear is large
items.question: The cartoon shows a small boat labelled Courage sailing toward a huge wave labelled Fear, while the sailor in the boat smiles and holds the tiller steady. The wave towers over the boat, but the boat does not turn back. What message does the cartoon most likely convey?

items.explanation: If the largest customer has already secured supply elsewhere, the firm can allocate scarce chips to smaller customers without losing its biggest account, which supports a fair allocation. A rival raising prices is a separate market fact. The chip maker offering a priority fee is a temptation, not a reason to favour one customer. The contract requiring equal treatment supports fairness but is a rule, not the commercial reason. A new chip design arriving later does not solve this quarter's shortage.
options: A rival firm has raised its prices because of the same shortage
The chip maker has offered a priority supply fee for faster delivery
The supply contract requires equal treatment of all customers
The largest customer has already secured an alternative supply for this quarter and will not be affected by a delay
A new chip design that uses fewer chips will be ready next year
items.passage: A maker of smart home devices needs a specialised chip that is now in short supply worldwide after a factory fire in another country. The firm has enough chips for only 40 percent of its planned production this quarter, and it must decide how to allocate them. Its largest customer, a retail chain, has ordered 50 percent of the planned output and is threatening to cancel all future orders if the firm does not meet the order in full. Three smaller customers, who together ordered 30 percent, have been loyal for years but have no alternative supplier. The remaining 20 percent is for the firm's own online store, which earns the highest margin per unit. The sales head wants to give all available chips to the largest customer to protect the relationship, arguing that losing the chain would cost the firm half its revenue. The operations head argues for a fair allocation across all customers, warning that abandoning loyal smaller customers will destroy trust and that the chain will return once supply recovers. The finance head notes that the online store earns the highest margin, so allocating chips there would protect profit. The chief executive must decide this week, because the chip shipment arrives on Monday and production planning cannot wait. The firm's 200 dealers have paid for showroom branding and have promised customers delivery dates that depend on the chip shipment arriving on Monday. The chip maker has said the next shipment will arrive in six weeks, but it cannot guarantee the quantity. The largest customer has threatened to cancel all future orders, which would cost the firm half its revenue, while the smaller customers have said they will wait if they are told honestly how long the delay will be.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support allocating the scarce chips fairly across all customers rather than giving them all to the largest customer?

items.explanation: A published allocation rule with a clear basis, a partial allocation to every customer, and a written timeline for the rest protects trust with all customers and gives the chain a reason to stay. Giving everything to the chain abandons loyal smaller customers. Giving everything to the online store maximises short-term margin but loses customers. An auction favours the richest buyer and breaks loyalty. Silence leaves every customer guessing.
options: Give all available chips to the largest customer and tell the smaller customers nothing
Give all available chips to the firm's own online store to maximise margin
Hold an auction and sell the chips to whichever customer bids the highest price
Wait until the next shipment arrives before telling any customer about the shortage
Allocate the available chips proportionally to every customer, publish the allocation rule and the timeline for the remaining orders, and offer the largest customer priority on the next shipment
items.question: Which allocation decision should the chief executive take this week?

items.explanation: If the chain has cancelled orders with other suppliers for smaller delays, the threat is credible and the case for prioritising the chain is stronger, which weakens the fair-allocation argument. The smaller customers being loyal supports fairness. The online margin and the chip maker fee do not address the chain's threat. A new design next year does not help this quarter.
options: The retail chain has cancelled orders with other suppliers in the past for delays far smaller than this one
The three smaller customers have been loyal for five years
The online store earns the highest margin per unit
The chip maker has offered a priority supply fee
A new chip design will be ready next year
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the operations head's argument for a fair allocation across all customers?

items.explanation: If the tracking data was sold to advertisers, the harm is concrete and the consent was never given, which makes the case for stopping the tracking decisive. The app being popular and parents liking the reports do not cure the lack of consent. A rival doing the same does not make it acceptable. The privacy policy mentioning partners in dense language is exactly the problem, since parents did not understand it.
options: The app is popular with parents who like the progress reports
The tracking data was sold to advertisers who target children with ads for games and snacks
A rival learning app also tracks how long children spend on each lesson
The privacy policy mentions sharing data with partners in dense legal language
The app is free for all schools that use it
items.passage: A learning app used by 5 lakh school children records how long each child spends on every lesson, which questions the child gets wrong, and the child's location while using the app. The app is free for schools, and its revenue comes from selling insights to advertisers and to publishers who want to know what children find difficult. The app's sign-up screen asks parents to agree to a long privacy policy, but the screen does not explain in plain language that children's learning data is sold. A journalist has found that the data includes enough detail to identify individual children when combined with school records, and has asked the company for a comment before publishing. The product head argues that the data helps publishers make better textbooks, that the app is free only because of this revenue, and that parents agreed to the policy. The child safety officer warns that selling children's data without clear consent breaches the trust of schools and parents, and that a regulator could ban the app from schools. The founders must decide before the journalist publishes, because the story will reach every school that uses the app. The journalist has given the company 48 hours to comment before publishing, and the story will reach every school that uses the app. The app is used in 2,000 schools and its progress reports are sent to parents every week. The child safety officer has warned that a regulator could ban the app from schools if children's data was sold without clear consent. The founders have told staff that the app will stay free only if the data revenue continues, and the company has no other source of income.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support stopping the sale of children's learning data?
items.set_title: DM2: The Learning App and Children's Data

items.explanation: If schools say they will remove the app if the story confirms data was sold, the revenue model itself is at risk, so stopping the sale protects the business as well as the children. The app being free is the reason for the sale, not a defence of it. Publishers wanting the data is a demand, not a justification. Parents agreeing to a dense policy is not informed consent. A future paid version is a plan, not evidence.
options: The app is free for schools only because of the revenue from selling data
Publishers say they want the learning data to improve textbooks
Schools that use the app say they will remove it if the story confirms that children's data was sold to advertisers
Parents agreed to the privacy policy when they signed up
The company plans to launch a paid version of the app next year
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support the child safety officer's view that the data sale must stop?
items.set_title: DM2: The Learning App and Children's Data

items.explanation: The app being free is a commercial reason the founders might hesitate, not a reason to stop the sale, so it is the exception. The sale to advertisers, the risk of identification, the schools threatening removal, the lack of clear consent, and the possible regulatory ban are all genuine reasons to stop.
options: The tracking data was sold to advertisers who target children
The data can identify individual children when combined with school records
Schools say they will remove the app if the sale is confirmed
The app is free for schools only because of this revenue
A regulator could ban the app from schools for selling children's data without clear consent
items.question: All of the following are valid reasons to stop selling the children's learning data EXCEPT
items.set_title: DM2: The Learning App and Children's Data

items.explanation: If the winning team used a leaked case from a previous year, the win was obtained unfairly and the case for disqualification is direct. The team being from a famous school and the judges praising the presentation do not cure cheating. A sponsor wanting a quick decision is a pressure, not a justification. The dean being new does not change the facts.
options: The winning team comes from a famous business school
The judges praised the winning team's presentation style
The main sponsor wants a decision before the press conference
The dean is new and wants to avoid controversy in the first year
The winning team used a leaked copy of the case from a previous year that other teams did not have
items.passage: A business school runs a national case competition with 40 teams and a prize of 10 lakh rupees, sponsored by a large bank. After the final, the organisers learn that the winning team may have received the case study in advance from a former student who now works at the sponsor bank. The evidence is a set of messages that suggest the team saw the case two days early, but the messages do not prove it beyond doubt. The dean must decide whether to disqualify the winning team, order a fresh final with a new case, or let the result stand. Disqualifying the team would embarrass the sponsor and the school, and the team has already been announced as the winner in the press. Ordering a fresh final would cost 15 lakh rupees and would be unfair to the other finalists who prepared for the original case. Letting the result stand would keep the sponsor happy but would leave the other 39 teams believing the competition was rigged. The dean has 48 hours before the prize ceremony, and the runner-up team has already written to the dean demanding an investigation. The runner-up team has written to the dean demanding an investigation and has shared its letter with the other finalists. The sponsor bank has said it wants the prize ceremony to go ahead as planned and has warned that a public dispute would damage its brand. The competition has run for 12 years and has never faced a cheating allegation before. The dean has 48 hours before the ceremony, and the winning team has already been announced in the press and on the school's website.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support disqualifying the winning team?

items.explanation: An independent investigation with the prize held back protects fairness without prejudging the team, and it gives the school a defensible basis for whatever follows. Disqualifying at once on unproven messages risks an injustice. Letting the result stand ignores the other teams. Asking the sponsor to decide is a conflict of interest, since the sponsor's employee is implicated. A private apology to the runner-up does not resolve the facts.
options: Hold the prize, commission a quick independent investigation by a panel that includes no one from the sponsor or the school, and act on its findings before the ceremony
Disqualify the winning team immediately on the basis of the messages alone
Let the result stand and hold the ceremony as planned
Ask the sponsor bank to decide whether its employee leaked the case
Apologise privately to the runner-up team and change nothing
items.question: What should the dean do?

items.explanation: If the former student sent the case to all finalists, the winning team had no advantage over the others, which directly undermines the case for disqualification. The team winning by a large margin does not show the win was fair. The sponsor's embarrassment and the cost of a fresh final are pressures, not evidence about fairness. The messages being unclear is a reason to investigate, not proof the team had no advantage.
options: The winning team won the final by a large margin
The former student sent the same case to all four finalist teams, not only to the winning team
The sponsor would be embarrassed by a disqualification
A fresh final would cost 15 lakh rupees
The messages do not prove beyond doubt that the team saw the case early
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the case for disqualifying the winning team?

items.explanation: If the two managers' teams have the highest attrition in the firm, the feud is already costing the firm its people, which strengthens the case for intervening now. Both managers being talented and both having long service explain why the firm hesitates, but do not show the feud is harmless. A client liking one manager is a reason to keep that person, not to ignore the conflict. The feud being about strategy is a description, not evidence that it is harmless.
options: Both managers are talented and have been with the firm for over ten years
The feud is about business strategy, not about personal issues
The two managers' teams have the highest staff attrition in the firm, with 12 people leaving in the last year
A major client likes working with one of the managers
Both managers have strong support among senior leadership
items.passage: Two senior managers in a consulting firm have been in open conflict for a year. One leads the digital practice and the other leads the traditional advisory practice, and each publicly criticises the other's work in front of clients and junior staff. Their teams have stopped sharing information, two joint projects have failed because the managers refused to cooperate, and 12 people have left the firm in the last year, most of them citing the conflict. The managing partner has so far avoided intervening, because both managers bring in large revenues and each has strong support among the partners. The human resources head warns that the conflict is now the main reason for attrition, that clients have noticed the tension, and that junior staff are afraid to work across the two practices. The managing partner must decide before the annual partner meeting, where the two managers are expected to argue again in front of all partners. The options are to mediate between them with a clear agreement, to separate their responsibilities completely, to remove one of them from a leadership role, or to do nothing and hope the conflict resolves itself. The managing partner has avoided intervening for a year because both managers bring in large revenues and each has strong support among the partners. The annual partner meeting is in three weeks, and the two managers are expected to argue again in front of all 40 partners. The human resources head has records of the 12 departures and of the two joint projects that failed when the managers refused to cooperate. Junior staff have told the human resources head they are afraid to work across the two practices.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support intervening now rather than waiting?
items.set_title: DM4: The Two Managers at War

items.explanation: If clients have already moved work to rivals because of the tension, the conflict is costing revenue now, which removes the main argument for tolerating it. The managers being talented is a reason to keep both, not to ignore the conflict. A joint project failing is evidence of harm but less direct than lost clients. The partner meeting being soon is a deadline, not a reason. Junior staff being afraid is a serious harm but the client loss is the commercial proof.
options: Both managers bring in large revenues for the firm
Two joint projects have failed because the managers refused to cooperate
The annual partner meeting is next month
Two major clients have moved work to rival firms, citing the tension between the managers
Junior staff are afraid to work across the two practices
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the managing partner's reason for not intervening, which is that both managers bring in large revenues?
items.set_title: DM4: The Two Managers at War

items.explanation: A mediated agreement with shared goals, joint accountability and a review date addresses the cooperation failure while keeping both managers, which is the proportionate first step. Doing nothing keeps the attrition. Separating the practices completely entrenches the split. Removing one manager at once is a last resort before mediation has been tried. Asking the managers to resolve it alone has already failed for a year.
options: Do nothing and hope the conflict resolves itself
Separate the two practices completely so the managers never need to work together
Remove one manager from a leadership role immediately
Ask the two managers to resolve the conflict on their own
Mediate between the managers with a written agreement on shared goals, joint accountability for shared projects, and a review after three months
items.question: What should the managing partner do first?
items.set_title: DM4: The Two Managers at War

items.explanation: If the rating system penalises drivers who refuse unsafe deliveries, the low ratings are caused by the firm's own rules, not by poor service, which supports changing the system. The drivers being independent contractors is a legal classification, not a reason to keep an unfair rating. Customers liking fast delivery is a preference, not evidence the rating is fair. A rival using a similar system does not make this one fair. The platform being popular does not show the rating is just.
options: The rating system penalises drivers who refuse deliveries that would require speeding or breaking traffic rules
The drivers are independent contractors, not employees of the platform
Customers like fast delivery and give low ratings to slow drivers
A rival platform uses a similar rating system
The platform is the most popular food delivery app in the city
items.passage: A food delivery platform rates its 8,000 riders on a five-star scale based on customer ratings, delivery time and order acceptance rate. Riders who fall below 4.2 stars lose access to the best delivery slots and earn 30 percent less, and riders below 3.8 stars are removed from the platform. Riders complain that the rating is unfair: customers give low ratings for late deliveries caused by traffic or by restaurants that are slow to prepare food, and the acceptance rate penalises riders who refuse orders that would require them to ride dangerously fast. The platform's operations head argues that the rating system keeps quality high, that customers have the right to rate, and that removing low-rated riders protects the brand. The rider welfare head argues that the system punishes riders for factors outside their control, that it pushes riders to break traffic rules to keep their rating, and that it should be changed to measure only what riders control. The chief executive must decide before the festive season, when order volumes double and rider earnings are at their highest. The festive season starts in four weeks, when order volumes double and rider earnings are at their highest for the year. Riders who fall below 4.2 stars lose access to the best delivery slots and earn 30 percent less, which is a large sum for people who depend on the platform for their living. The platform has 8,000 riders in the city and its operations head has said the rating system is the main tool for keeping quality high. The rider welfare head has collected 500 complaints about unfair ratings in the last three months.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support changing the rating system?

items.explanation: If riders who were removed had higher customer satisfaction than those who stayed, the rating is measuring the wrong thing, which directly undermines the claim that it protects quality. The platform being popular and customers having a right to rate do not show the rating is accurate. A rival system and the festive season are not evidence about accuracy.
options: The platform is the most popular food delivery app in the city

Riders who were removed for low ratings had higher customer satisfaction scores on food quality and politeness than riders who stayed, and were removed mainly for late deliveries caused by restaurants
Customers have the right to rate the service they receive
A rival platform uses a similar rating system
Order volumes double during the festive season
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the operations head's claim that the rating system keeps quality high?

items.explanation: Customers having a right to rate is a reason to keep some customer feedback, not a reason to change the system, so it is the exception. Punishing riders for traffic and restaurant delays, pushing riders to break traffic rules, removing riders for factors outside their control, and the link between low ratings and a 30 percent pay cut are all genuine reasons to change the system.
options: The rating punishes riders for late deliveries caused by traffic and slow restaurants
The system pushes riders to break traffic rules to protect their rating
Customers have the right to rate the service they receive
Riders below 3.8 stars are removed for factors outside their control
A low rating cuts a rider's earnings by 30 percent through lost access to the best slots
items.question: All of the following are valid reasons to change the rating system EXCEPT

items.explanation: If the platform's own audit found that a third of five-star reviews came from paid accounts, the fakery is proven by the firm's own data, which makes the case for removing them decisive. The sellers being small businesses and the reviews helping sales are pressures, not justifications. A rival having fake reviews does not make this firm's reviews honest. The audit being expensive is a cost, not evidence.
options: The sellers are mostly small businesses that depend on the platform
Fake reviews help the sellers increase their sales
A rival platform also has fake reviews
The platform's own audit found that a third of the five-star reviews for the top sellers came from paid accounts that never bought the products
An independent audit would cost a large sum
items.passage: An e-commerce platform has discovered that many of its top sellers have bought thousands of five-star reviews from agencies that post fake reviews for a fee. The fake reviews push these sellers to the top of search results, while honest sellers with genuine four-star reviews are buried on later pages. Customers who bought from the top sellers have complained that the products were far worse than the reviews suggested, and a consumer group is threatening to report the platform to the regulator. The platform's trust head wants to remove all fake reviews, ban the sellers who bought them, and publish a clear policy. The commercial head warns that the top sellers generate 40 percent of the platform's revenue, that banning them would cut revenue sharply, and that customers rarely check whether reviews are genuine. The chief executive must decide before the festive sale, when the platform earns a third of its annual revenue and the fake reviews will influence the most purchases. The consumer group has collected 3,000 complaints from customers who bought products that were far worse than the reviews suggested, and it plans to report the platform to the regulator next week. The festive sale starts in three weeks and the platform earns a third of its annual revenue during that period. The top sellers who bought reviews generate 40 percent of the platform's revenue, while honest sellers with genuine four-star reviews are buried on later pages of search results. The trust head has asked for a budget to audit reviews every month. The commercial head has warned that banning the top sellers would cut revenue sharply and could lead to job losses in the sales team.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support removing the fake reviews and banning the sellers who bought them?

items.explanation: Removing fake reviews, banning repeat offenders, and showing a verified-purchase badge gives customers honest information while keeping honest sellers, and it protects the platform from the regulator. Doing nothing leaves customers misled. Removing reviews only for small sellers is unfair. Warning sellers privately without action changes nothing. Paying for more reviews repeats the problem.
options: Do nothing and let the festive sale run with the fake reviews in place
Remove fake reviews only for small sellers and leave the top sellers untouched
Warn the sellers privately but take no public action
Pay an agency to post genuine-looking reviews for honest sellers
Remove the fake reviews, ban sellers who repeatedly buy reviews, mark all remaining reviews with a verified-purchase badge, and publish the policy before the festive sale
items.question: What should the chief executive do before the festive sale?

items.explanation: If honest sellers say they will leave the platform unless the fake reviews are removed, inaction loses the sellers the platform needs most, which weakens the commercial case for keeping the top sellers. The top sellers generating 40 percent of revenue supports keeping them. Customers rarely checking reviews supports the commercial head. A regulator fine and customer complaints both support removal.
options: Honest sellers say they will leave the platform unless the fake reviews are removed
The top sellers generate 40 percent of the platform's revenue
Customers rarely check whether reviews are genuine
The regulator could fine the platform for misleading customers
Customers have complained that products were far worse than the reviews suggested
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the commercial head's argument for keeping the top sellers who bought fake reviews?

items.explanation: If the airline's own data shows that most passengers book only a week before travel, the last-minute price rise hits the majority, which supports capping it. The airline being profitable and the rival doing the same do not justify the practice. Empty seats being filled at high prices is a revenue gain, not a fairness argument. A regulator inquiry is a risk, not proof of the harm.
options: The airline is profitable and does not need the extra revenue
The airline's own data shows that most passengers on this route book only a week before travel, when the price has already doubled
A rival airline also doubles its prices in the last week
The last-minute seats are mostly bought by business travellers
The regulator has opened an inquiry into airline pricing
items.passage: A domestic airline has introduced dynamic pricing on a popular route, and fares in the last week before departure are now double the price charged three months earlier. The route is used mainly by families visiting relatives and by students returning home, and many passengers have complained that they cannot plan or afford the trip. The airline's revenue head argues that dynamic pricing fills seats efficiently, that passengers who book early pay less, and that the practice is standard across the industry. The customer service head warns that the price rise looks like profiteering, that the airline's brand is built on being affordable for ordinary families, and that a rival airline has kept its prices flat on the same route. The chief executive must decide before the holiday season, when demand on the route triples and the last-week fares will be at their highest. The airline's board is split, and the regulator has asked the airline to explain its pricing. The holiday season starts in six weeks, when demand on the route triples and last-week fares will be at their highest. The route is used mainly by families visiting relatives and by students returning home, many of whom cannot book months in advance. The board is split, with half the directors supporting the revenue head and half supporting the customer service head. The regulator has asked the airline to explain its pricing and has said it may publish the airline's response. A rival airline has kept its prices flat on the same route. The customer service team has received 4,000 complaints about the fare rise in the last month, mostly from families who say they can no longer afford the trip.
items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support capping the last-week fare increase?

items.explanation: A cap on the last-week increase with early-bird fares kept low protects ordinary families while preserving the incentive to book early, which balances revenue and fairness. Keeping the doubled fares ignores the brand harm. A flat fare for all removes the early-booking incentive. A last-week discount for everyone destroys revenue. Doing nothing until the regulator acts leaves the brand exposed.
options: Keep the doubled last-week fares and ignore the complaints
Introduce a flat fare for all passengers regardless of when they book
Cap the last-week fare at 30 percent above the early-bird fare, publish the fare bands in advance, and keep a small number of seats at the lowest fare for students and families
Offer a discount on last-week fares to every passenger who asks for one
Do nothing until the regulator orders a change
items.question: What should the chief executive do before the holiday season?

items.explanation: Dynamic pricing filling seats efficiently is a commercial benefit to the airline, not a criticism of the cap, so it is the exception. The harm to families, the brand built on affordability, the rival keeping prices flat, the regulator's inquiry, and the fact that most passengers cannot book early are all genuine criticisms of the doubled last-week fare.
options: Dynamic pricing fills seats efficiently and rewards early booking
The fare rise hits families and students who cannot book months in advance
The airline's brand is built on being affordable for ordinary families
A rival airline has kept its prices flat on the same route
The regulator has asked the airline to explain its pricing
items.question: All of the following are valid criticisms of the doubled last-week fare EXCEPT
A dealer purchases a watch for Rs 1200. He marks it 50% above the cost price and then offers a discount of 25%. What is his profit percentage on the transaction?
items.explanation: The marked price is Rs 1200 x 1.50 = Rs 1800. After the 25% discount the selling price is Rs 1800 x 0.75 = Rs 1350, a profit of Rs 150 on Rs 1200, which is 12.5%. The naive 25% answer ignores that the discount is charged on the higher marked price.

items.question: Two runners start together from the same point on a circular track of length 1200 metres and run in the same direction at 10 m/s and 8 m/s. After how many minutes do they meet for the first time?
options: 10 minutes
8 minutes
12 minutes
6 minutes
15 minutes
items.explanation: The faster runner gains 2 m/s on the slower one and must gain a full lap of 1200 m to meet again. The time is 1200/2 = 600 seconds, which is 10 minutes. Dividing by the sum of the speeds would be correct only if they ran in opposite directions.

items.question: The ages of three friends are 24, 31 and 29 years. What is their average age?
options: 27 years
28 years
29 years
26 years
30 years
items.explanation: The sum of the ages is 84 years, so the average is 84/3 = 28 years. The middle value and the range of the ages are not the average, and rounding the sum first gives the wrong options.

items.question: Seven boxes have distinct positive integer weights in kg, and their average weight is 15 kg. What is the maximum possible value of the largest weight?
items.explanation: The sum of all 7 values is 7 x 15 = 105. To make the largest value as big as possible, the other 6 values must be as small as possible while staying distinct and positive, so they are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, summing to 21. The largest value is therefore 105 - 21 = 84. Forgetting that the values must be distinct, or using the average itself as the maximum, gives the wrong options.

items.question: Pipe A can fill a tank in 8 hours while pipe B can empty the full tank in 12 hours. If both pipes are opened together when the tank is empty, in how many hours will the tank be filled?
options: 20 hours
24 hours
16 hours
10 hours
12 hours
items.explanation: A fills 1/8 of the tank per hour and B empties 1/12, so the net fill rate is 1/8 - 1/12 = 1/24 per hour. The tank therefore takes 24 hours to fill. Adding the rates instead of subtracting them would wrongly give about 4.8 hours.

items.question: What is the perimeter of a semicircle of radius 14 cm? (Use pi = 22/7)
options: 44 cm
88 cm
72 cm
58 cm
100 cm
items.explanation: The curved part is half the circumference, (22/7) x 14 = 44 cm, and the straight diameter adds 28 cm. The total perimeter is 44 + 28 = 72 cm. Counting only the curved part, or the full circumference, gives the wrong options.

items.question: What is the maximum area of a rectangle that can be inscribed in a semicircle of radius 10 cm, with one side on the diameter?
options: 200 sq cm
50 sq cm
157 sq cm
80 sq cm
100 sq cm
items.explanation: Let the rectangle have half-width x and height y with x squared + y squared = 10 squared. Its area is 2xy, which is largest when x = y = 10/sqrt(2), giving an area of 10 squared = 100 sq cm. A rectangle using the full diameter as its base cannot reach this area.

items.question: An isosceles triangle has a base of 16 cm and each of its equal sides is 10 cm long. What is its area?
options: 80 sq cm
60 sq cm
40 sq cm
48 sq cm
96 sq cm
items.explanation: The altitude to the base bisects it, so the height is sqrt(10 squared - 8 squared) = sqrt(36) = 6 cm. The area is (1/2) x 16 x 6 = 48 sq cm. Using the equal side as the height gives the wrong options.

items.question: A tower stands on level ground. From a point 20 m from its base the angle of elevation of the top is 60 degrees. From a point 40 m further away on the same line, the angle of elevation is 30 degrees. Both observations are consistent with the same tower height. What is the height of the tower?
items.explanation: Let the height be h and the nearer distance be x. Then tan 60 = h/x and tan 30 = h/(x+40). From the first, h = x sqrt(3); substituting in the second gives x = 20 m, so h = 20 sqrt(3) m, about 34.64 m. Using only one observation with the wrong distance gives the wrong options.

items.question: What is the volume of a cuboid of length 12 cm, breadth 8 cm and height 6 cm?
options: 576 cubic cm
480 cubic cm
672 cubic cm
600 cubic cm
720 cubic cm
items.explanation: The volume is length x breadth x height = 12 x 8 x 6 = 576 cubic cm. The surface area is a different quantity, and multiplying only two of the dimensions gives the wrong options.

items.question: How many integers from 1 to 100 are divisible by 3 or by 5?
items.explanation: There are 33 multiples of 3 and 20 multiples of 5 up to 100, but the 6 multiples of 15 are counted twice. By inclusion-exclusion the count is 33 + 20 - 6 = 47. Adding the two counts without correcting for the overlap gives the wrong options.

items.question: How many four-digit numbers are divisible by 12, 15 and 18?
items.explanation: A number divisible by 12, 15 and 18 is a multiple of their LCM, 180. The four-digit multiples run from 1080 = 6 x 180 to 55 x 180 = 9900, which is 55 - 5 = 50 numbers. Counting the multiples below 1000 as well would give the wrong options.

items.question: How many trailing zeroes does 100! have?
items.explanation: The number of trailing zeroes in n! is the count of factors of 5. For n = 100 this is 20 + 4 + 0 + 0 = 24. Counting only the multiples of 5, or counting multiples of 10, gives the wrong options.

items.question: What is the largest integer n such that n squared is less than 5000 and n is divisible by 7?
items.explanation: Since sqrt(5000) is about 70.7, n can be at most 70. The largest multiple of 7 not exceeding 70 is 70 itself, and 70 squared = 4900 is less than 5000. The next multiple, 77, has a square above 5000, so it fails.

items.question: If alpha + beta = 7 and alpha x beta = 10, what is alpha squared + beta squared?
items.explanation: Alpha squared + beta squared = (alpha + beta) squared - 2 alpha beta = 7 squared - 2 x 10 = 49 - 20 = 29. Simply squaring the sum, or adding the product, gives the wrong options.

items.question: If x + y = 10 with x and y positive real numbers, what is the maximum possible value of xy?
items.explanation: By AM-GM, xy is at most ((x + y)/2) squared = 5 squared = 25, with equality when x = y = 5. The product is smaller whenever the two numbers are unequal, so the other options, which are products of unequal pairs summing to 10, are all below the maximum.

items.question: A fair coin is tossed 4 times. What is the probability of getting exactly 2 heads?
items.explanation: There are 2 to the power 4 = 16 equally likely sequences, and exactly 2 heads can occur in C(4,2) = 6 ways, so the probability is 6/16 = 3/8. The probability of at least 2 heads, or of exactly 1 head, gives the wrong options.

items.question: In a class of 80 students, 45 play cricket, 38 play football and 12 play both games. How many students play neither game?
items.explanation: The number playing at least one game is 45 + 38 - 12 = 71, since the 12 who play both are counted twice. So the number playing neither is 80 - 71 = 9. Adding the two counts without subtracting the overlap gives the wrong options.

items.question: What is the two-digit number? Statement I: The sum of its digits is 9. Statement II: The difference of its digits is 3.
options: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient.
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither statement alone is sufficient.
Either statement alone is sufficient.
Neither statement alone nor both together are sufficient.
items.explanation: The digits could be 6 and 3, giving 63, or 3 and 6, giving 36: both have digit sum 9 and digit difference 3. Even together the statements leave two possible numbers, so neither statement alone nor both together are sufficient.

items.question: What is the total exports to the five countries in 2024?

diagram.caption: Exports (USD billion) to five countries, 2023 and 2024

options: USD 149 billion
USD 169 billion
USD 159 billion
USD 154 billion
USD 164 billion
items.explanation: Adding the 2024 column gives 52 + 41 + 28 + 21 + 17 = USD 159 billion. The 2023 total is 138 billion, which is a distractor.

items.question: Which country recorded the highest percentage growth in exports from 2023 to 2024?
options: USA
China
UK
UAE
Germany
items.explanation: The growth rates are USA 15.56%, China 7.89%, UAE 27.27%, UK 16.67% and Germany 13.33%, so UAE grew fastest. The USA has the largest absolute increase, but the question asks for percentage growth.

items.question: What percentage of the total 2024 exports went to the USA?
items.explanation: The USA received USD 52 billion of the USD 159 billion total, which is 52/159 x 100 = 32.7%. Using the 2023 figures, or the USA share of a different total, gives the wrong options.

items.question: What is the total sales across all regions in 2025?
options: Rs 500 crore
Rs 580 crore
Rs 520 crore
Rs 540 crore
Rs 560 crore
items.explanation: Adding the 2025 figures gives 140 + 160 + 110 + 130 = Rs 540 crore. The 2024 total is 470 crore, which is a distractor.

items.question: Which region recorded the highest percentage growth in sales from 2024 to 2025?
options: North
South
East
West
All four regions are equal
items.explanation: The growth rates are North 16.67%, South 6.67%, East 22.22% and West 18.18%, so East grew fastest. The South has the highest sales in both years, but its growth rate is the lowest.

items.question: What is the overall percentage growth in total sales from 2024 to 2025?
items.explanation: Total sales rose from Rs 470 crore to Rs 540 crore, an increase of Rs 70 crore, which is 14.89%. Averaging the four regional growth rates gives a different figure, which is wrong because the regions have different sizes.

items.question: How many orders were returned in total across the three categories?

diagram.caption: Orders and return rates in three product categories
diagram.content: An e-commerce firm received 4000 orders for Electronics with a return rate of 10%, 6000 orders for Clothing with a return rate of 15%, and 5000 orders for Grocery with a return rate of 5%.

options: 1400 orders
1550 orders
1700 orders
1450 orders
1650 orders
items.explanation: Returns are Electronics: 400, Clothing: 900 and Grocery: 250, totalling 1550 orders. Adding the return rates, or using the gross order count, gives the wrong options.

items.question: Which category had the largest number of returned orders?
options: Electronics
Grocery
Clothing
Electronics and Grocery
All three are equal
items.explanation: Returned orders are Electronics 400, Clothing 900 and Grocery 250, so Clothing had the most returns. Clothing has both the most orders and the highest return rate, so it leads on both counts.

items.question: How many orders were delivered without being returned?
options: 12950 orders
13950 orders
13450 orders
13200 orders
13700 orders
items.explanation: Total orders were 15000 and 1550 were returned, so 15000 - 1550 = 13450 orders were delivered without return. The gross order count, or the return count alone, gives the wrong options.

items.question: The 2025 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded for discoveries concerning peripheral immune tolerance. Which trio shared the prize?
options: Mary Brunkow, Fred Ramsdell and Shimon Sakaguchi
Katalin Kariko, Drew Weissman and Robert Langer
Svante Paabo, David Julius and Ardem Patapoutian
Harvey Alter, Michael Houghton and Charles Rice
James Allison, Tasuku Honjo and Gregg Semenza
items.explanation: Mary Brunkow, Fred Ramsdell and Shimon Sakaguchi shared the 2025 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries about peripheral immune tolerance and regulatory T cells. Kariko and Weissman won in 2023 for mRNA vaccines, Paabo in 2022 for ancient genomes, the Alter trio in 2020 for hepatitis C, and Allison and Honjo in 2018 for cancer immunotherapy.

items.question: Who won the Asia Cup cricket tournament in 2025?
options: Pakistan
India
Sri Lanka
Bangladesh
Afghanistan
items.explanation: India won the Asia Cup in 2025, beating Pakistan in the final in Dubai in September 2025. Pakistan finished runner-up, while Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Afghanistan were eliminated before the final.

items.question: Who was sworn in as the President of the United States in January 2025?
options: Joe Biden
Kamala Harris
Donald Trump
Barack Obama
Mike Pence
items.explanation: Donald Trump was sworn in as President of the United States on 20 January 2025, beginning his second term. Joe Biden was the outgoing President, Kamala Harris lost the 2024 election, Barack Obama left office in 2017, and Mike Pence was Vice President from 2017 to 2021.

items.question: Who won the ICC World Test Championship final in 2025?
options: Australia
India
England
South Africa
New Zealand
items.explanation: South Africa won the 2025 ICC World Test Championship final, beating Australia at Lord's in June 2025 for its first title. Australia were the defending champions, India did not reach the final, and England and New Zealand were not finalists.

items.question: At the 71st National Film Awards announced in 2025, who won the Best Actor award for the film Jawan?
options: Vikrant Massey
Ranbir Kapoor
Vicky Kaushal
Allu Arjun
Shah Rukh Khan
items.explanation: Shah Rukh Khan won the Best Actor award for Jawan at the 71st National Film Awards, sharing the honour with Vikrant Massey, who won for 12th Fail. Massey won for a different film, while Ranbir Kapoor, Vicky Kaushal and Allu Arjun did not win Best Actor that year.

items.question: Who won the FIDE Women's World Cup in 2025?
options: Divya Deshmukh
Koneru Humpy
Harika Dronavalli
Vaishali Rameshbabu
Ju Wenjun
items.explanation: Divya Deshmukh won the FIDE Women's World Cup in 2025, beating Koneru Humpy in the final in Batumi in July 2025. Humpy finished runner-up, Ju Wenjun is the Women's World Champion but did not win this event, and Harika Dronavalli and Vaishali Rameshbabu were eliminated earlier.

items.question: In June 2025, the Reserve Bank of India cut the repo rate to which level?
options: 6.5 percent
5.5 percent
6.0 percent
5.0 percent
4.75 percent
items.explanation: The Reserve Bank of India cut the repo rate by 50 basis points to 5.5 percent in June 2025. The rate had been 6.0 percent after the April 2025 cut and 6.5 percent through 2024, while 5.0 percent and 4.75 percent were never reached in 2025.

items.question: Which club won the UEFA Champions League in 2025?
options: Real Madrid
Inter Milan
Paris Saint-Germain
Manchester City
Bayern Munich
items.explanation: Paris Saint-Germain won the 2025 UEFA Champions League, beating Inter Milan 5-0 in the final in Munich for the club's first title. Inter Milan finished runner-up, Real Madrid were eliminated in the quarter-finals, and Manchester City and Bayern Munich did not reach the final.

items.question: The COP30 climate summit in November 2025 was held in which country?
options: Egypt
United Arab Emirates
Azerbaijan
Brazil
India
items.explanation: COP30 was held in Belem, Brazil, in November 2025. Egypt hosted COP27, the United Arab Emirates hosted COP28, and Azerbaijan hosted COP29, while India has never hosted a COP summit.

items.question: Who was conferred the Jnanpith Award announced in 2025?
options: Gulzar
Amitav Ghosh
Damodar Mauzo
Krishna Sobti
Vinod Kumar Shukla
